questions.stimulusTitle: Why Some Bridges Have Expansion Joints
questions.stimulusText:
A bridge may appear solid and motionless, but its materials expand and contract as temperatures change. Steel and concrete become slightly larger when warmed and slightly smaller when cooled.
If a long bridge had no room for this movement, repeated temperature changes could place stress on its structure. Engineers therefore include expansion joints at selected locations. These joints create small gaps or flexible connections that allow parts of the bridge to move without pushing dangerously against one another.
The amount of movement depends on several factors, including the bridge's length, the materials used, and the range of temperatures expected in the region. A short bridge in a mild climate may require less movement space than a much longer bridge exposed to very hot summers and cold winters.
Expansion joints must also handle traffic. Cars and trucks pass over them repeatedly, so joints are designed to support loads while still allowing controlled motion. They require inspection because dirt, ice, or worn parts can reduce how well they function.
The joints are therefore not signs of weakness. They are deliberate features that help a rigid-looking structure respond safely to natural changes in temperature.

questions.stimulusText:
An archive is often imagined as a place filled with rare documents: signed letters, old photographs, official records, and carefully preserved books. Those materials can be valuable, but an archive's usefulness depends on more than the age or rarity of what it contains.
Researchers need context. A single photograph may show a crowded street, yet without a date, location, or explanation, its meaning can be difficult to determine. A simple receipt or handwritten schedule may seem ordinary, but if it identifies a business, event, or daily routine, it can help researchers understand a larger pattern.
Organization also matters. Materials that cannot be located are difficult to study. Archivists therefore create descriptions, labels, and finding aids that connect individual items to people, places, dates, and subjects.
Preservation is another part of the work. Documents must be protected from moisture, light, pests, and rough handling. Increasingly, archives also preserve digital files, which create different challenges because formats and storage systems can become outdated.
A useful archive, then, is not merely a room full of old objects. It is a collection whose materials are preserved, organized, and described well enough for people to ask meaningful questions about the past.

questions.explanation: Jonah explicitly says that he keeps rushing a particular section.
questions.stimulusText:
Mara had practiced the opening of her piano duet so many times that she could hear every measure before her fingers touched the keys. Yet during the final rehearsal, her partner, Jonah, stopped halfway through the second page.
“I keep rushing this part,” he said, pointing to a row of quick notes.
Mara glanced at the clock. Their recital was the next evening, and she wanted one flawless run before leaving. She suggested starting again from the beginning.
Their teacher, Mr. Bell, shook his head. Instead, he asked them to play only the troublesome four measures, first at half speed. Mara felt impatient. The opening was already polished, and repeating a tiny section seemed less satisfying than completing the whole piece.
After several slow attempts, however, Jonah stopped rushing. More surprisingly, Mara noticed that she had been entering one beat too early after his phrase. The mistake had been small enough to hide whenever they played quickly.
They practiced the four measures again, then connected them to the music before and after. On the final run, neither student tried to race toward the ending. The duet felt steadier than it ever had.
As Mara packed her music, she realized that a complete performance had not been what they needed most. Their best rehearsal had come from spending time on the smallest unfinished part.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Quiet Work of Seed Banks
questions.stimulusText:
A seed bank stores seeds so that plant varieties can be preserved for future study and use. Collections may include seeds from crops, wild relatives of crops, and plants adapted to particular climates or soils.
Storage begins long before a container is placed on a shelf. Staff members document where seeds came from and identify the plant variety as accurately as possible. Many seeds are dried to reduce moisture and then kept at low temperatures, conditions that can slow biological processes and extend storage life.
Stored seeds do not remain useful forever without attention. Workers periodically test samples to see how many seeds still germinate. If germination rates fall too low, staff may grow plants from the remaining viable seeds and collect a fresh generation for storage. This process must be managed carefully so that the renewed sample continues to represent the original variety.
Seed banks are sometimes described as insurance against crop loss, but their role is broader. Researchers can use stored material to study traits such as disease resistance, drought tolerance, or adaptation to local conditions. Plant breeders may also use preserved varieties when developing new crops.
A seed bank is therefore both a storage facility and an active scientific resource. Its value depends not merely on keeping seeds cold, but on maintaining accurate records, monitoring viability, and preserving useful genetic diversity over time.

questions.stimulusText:
Mr. Chen's photography club usually walked the same path through the neighborhood park. The route passed a pond, a stone bridge, and a row of old sycamores, all dependable subjects for beginning photographers.
One Saturday, construction closed the bridge. Several students groaned when Mr. Chen led them along a narrow side trail instead. The path seemed ordinary at first, bordered by shrubs and a plain wooden fence.
Then Lila noticed sunlight passing through a tear in one leaf, casting a bright oval on the fence. She crouched to photograph it. Farther ahead, another student found repeating shadows made by bicycle spokes at a repair station. Soon the group was stopping every few steps.
Mr. Chen did not point out subjects. Instead, he asked questions: Where does your eye go first? What changes if you move two steps to the left? Which detail would someone else overlook?
By the time the group reached the far side of the park, no one was complaining about the detour. Lila had taken fewer photographs than usual, but she had spent more time deciding what each picture should include.
At the next meeting, Mr. Chen displayed photographs from both the familiar route and the detour. The strongest images, he observed, were not tied to the most impressive scenery. They came from photographers who had learned to notice deliberately.

A bridge may appear solid and motionless, yet its materials change slightly as temperatures rise and fall. Many materials expand when warmed and contract when cooled. Over a long structure, even small changes in length can matter.

These joints allow parts of the structure to move a limited amount without forcing the entire bridge to resist that movement.

questions.stimulusTitle: How Desert Plants Limit Water Loss
questions.stimulusText:
Plants living in dry environments face a difficult problem: they need sunlight and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, yet exchanging gases with the air can also allow water vapor to escape. Desert plants have evolved several features that help manage this tradeoff.
Many have a waxy outer coating that slows evaporation from exposed surfaces. Some also have small or narrow leaves, reducing the surface area from which water can be lost. In certain species, leaves are replaced by spines while green stems perform much of the photosynthesis.
Another adaptation involves stomata, tiny openings that regulate gas exchange. Most plants open their stomata mainly during the day. Some desert plants, however, open them primarily at night, when temperatures are lower and the air may be less drying. They store carbon-containing compounds produced from the nighttime gas exchange and use them during daylight for photosynthesis.
These adaptations do not eliminate the need for water. Roots must still absorb moisture, and prolonged drought can stress even highly adapted species. Instead, the features reduce unnecessary water loss and help plants make use of limited supplies.
A desert plant's survival therefore depends not on a single unusual trait but on several coordinated features. Shape, surface coverings, gas-exchange timing, and root function can all contribute to conserving a resource that is difficult to replace.

questions.stimulusText:
Before satellite images and digital mapping tools, mapmakers often depended on measurements collected directly in the field. A surveyor might record distances, directions, elevations, landmarks, road conditions, and the positions of rivers or buildings. These observations were then compared and converted into maps.
Field notebooks were essential to this work. A page might contain neat columns of measurements beside hurried sketches, abbreviations, weather notes, or reminders to check a doubtful reading. Such notebooks were working documents rather than polished publications.
Their imperfections can make them valuable to historians. A finished map shows the result of a mapping project, but field notes may reveal how that result was produced. Crossed-out numbers can show that a measurement was reconsidered. Repeated visits to one location may suggest that the terrain was difficult to survey. Notes about a washed-out road or a newly built bridge can also preserve details about a landscape at a particular moment.
Historians must still interpret these records carefully. A surveyor could make an error, use an unfamiliar abbreviation, or omit information that seemed obvious at the time. One notebook should not automatically be treated as complete evidence.
Even so, field notes provide something a finished map often cannot: a record of decisions, uncertainty, and revision. They show mapping not simply as the creation of a product, but as a process of observing and checking the world.

Crossed-out numbers can show that a measurement was reconsidered. Repeated visits to one location may suggest that the terrain was difficult to survey. Notes about a washed-out road or a newly built bridge can also preserve details about a landscape at a particular moment.
Historians must still interpret these records carefully. A surveyor could make an error, use an unfamiliar abbreviation, or omit information that seemed obvious at the time. One notebook should not automatically be treated as complete evidence.
Even so, field notes provide something a finished map often cannot: a record of decisions, uncertainty, and revision. They show mapping not simply as the creation of a product, but as a process of observing and checking the world.
